To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
DNA methylation defects at imprinted loc are rare in children born small for gestation age.
we found DNA methylation changes in 6 out of 98 children born SGA at single imprinted loci.

we found that aberrant DNA methylation at imputed loci in children with growth retardation is rare and that the diagnosis of a rare imprinting disorder can be established in a child with growth retardation by DNA methylation analysis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of the epigenome of patients born small for their gestational age (SAGA).
the identification of epimutation in children born SCA.
the analysis of epigenetic defects in patients born small for their gestational age (birth weight below the 10th percentile).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the DNA methylation analysis of imprinted genes should be included in the diagnostic work-up of children born SGA, but the clinical impact of this analysis is currently limited.
the frequency of DNA methylation abnormalities at imprinted loc in SGA children is very low.
epigenetic defects in patients with SGA should be considered but are not a major cause of this phenotype.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
epimutations in children born SCA are rare but do exist.
the detection of epimutations at imprinting genes should be part of the diagnostic workup in children born SCA.
epimutation in the MEG3 DMR in 14q is a rare event, and the clinical consequences of the epimutation of IGF2R in 6q is not clear.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the diagnosis of imprinting disorders in children born SCA is not straightforward.
the detection of epigenetic alterations in children born SCA is possible, but rare.
DNA methylation changes are rare in children born small for gestation age (SGA) but can be identified in a subset of patients.
